name: Blush
lede: Blush is the colour of flushed skin, and the word has two lives: in Paterson's dictionary it runs from red to a delicate pink, and in St Clair's glossary to a pinkish beige, while the swatch on this site is a much deeper pink.

sections.title: A word for a face
sections.body:
*Blush* is first a verb: to change the colour of the face when embarrassed, stressed or angry [1]. As a colour word it follows from that, and Paterson's dictionary gives it as red-coloured, with *blush pink* as a delicate pink and *blush rose* as a delicate pink that is also sometimes a dark shade of rose [1]. A cosmetic that adds colour to the cheeks is a *blusher* [1].

St Clair's glossary of colour names defines blush as a pinkish beige, like flushed cheeks [3]. The older word *damask* was used in the same way, glossed by Paterson as a deep pink or rose, "blush-coloured" [2].

sections.title: Shame, skin and paint
sections.body:
The idea behind the word is old. Greenfield notes that the ancient Jews linked red with the plainest act of shame and self-betrayal, the blush [4]. A twelfth-century description of a mosaic in the Great Palace at Constantinople, by Constantine Manasses, praised painting over sculpture because shading could show the roughness of skin and every complexion, a blush among them [5].

Finlay, writing about an icon painter's natural pigments, reports the Orthodox view that grinding a piece of natural rock into the blush on a saint's cheek parallels a human transformation [6].

sections.title: Which blush is this?
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is #DE5D83, a clear mid pink, and it is deeper than the delicate pinks the dictionaries describe [7]. Our library holds it as a name from ISCC-NBS (1955, block 29) and Maerz and Paul (1930), and notes that Wikipedia cites Crayola for it [7]. The Maerz and Paul entry carries a first-recorded year of 1590, which we give as that book's claim and have not checked elsewhere [7].

The nearest named colour is [[cerise]], at a ΔE of 8.5, so it is a pink with some depth [7]. A second source disagrees about what the name means: the xkcd colour survey of 2010 gives blush as a soft peach, #F29E8E [7]. The paler, skin-like colours are better matched by [[blush-pink]], [[salmon-pink]] and [[peach]], and the deeper ones by [[rose]] and [[old-rose]] [7]. In Paterson's entries, the paler uses are the *blush pink* and *blush rose* ones, not this swatch [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this exact pink covering at least one per cent of its canvas, within a CIEDE2000 distance of 4 [8]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and the archive is made of photographs of aged, varnished paintings [8].

The peach version of blush is rarer still in size but easier to find in the right hands. A colour within six units of #F29E8E covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 7 paintings [9]. The two largest are [[painter:andre-derain|Derain]]'s *Woman in a Chemise* (1906), at 23 per cent of the picture, and [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]]'s *Odalisque* (1923), at 20 per cent [9]. Both are paintings of bare or lightly dressed skin [9].

In Google Books, the word *blush* is at its highest in the earliest decade we have, 1800, fell to about a tenth of that by the 1970s, and had recovered to about 42 per cent of the 1800 level by 2010 [10]. That count includes the verb and the flower and cosmetic senses, so it is the history of a word, not only of a colour [10].

questions.q: In Paterson's dictionary, what is blush pink?
Why is the swatch on this page a poor guide to the word's usual meaning?
choices: It is a clear mid pink, far deeper than the pale tint the word names
It is exactly the colour of a painted cheek
It has no name in any source
questions.answer: It is a clear mid pink, far deeper than the pale tint the word names

questions.q: True or false: the word blush began as a colour name rather than a verb for a flushed face.

openers: Blush began as a verb for a face going red, and the colour words came after.
The deep pink swatch here is not the delicate pink that Paterson gives for blush pink.
